title: Vetala Story 7: The Prince Who Would Not Marry
summary: The Vetala said: 'Listen, O King, to the riddle of Prince Gunakara, who refused every royal bride!'...
keywords: vetala story 7: the prince who would not marry
full_text:
Through the whistling cemetery wind, King Vikramaditya recaptured the corpse and carried it once more upon his back.

The Vetala said: 'Listen, O King, to the riddle of Prince Gunakara, who refused every royal bride!'

In the kingdom of Kashi, Prince Gunakara reached his twenty-fifth year, handsome, athletic, and deeply versed in the arts. His father, the Emperor, presented him with portraits of princesses from fifty kingdoms, urging him to wed.

The prince refused them all, declaring: 'Father, common men marry for physical beauty, but beauty without moral virtue is a gilded cage containing a serpent! I will marry only that maiden who can solve three philosophical riddles of virtue!'

Four noble princesses arrived to contest for his hand: Princess Chandra of Avanti, Princess Ratna of Kalinga, Princess Padma of Magadha, and Princess Kanti of Kosala.

The prince posed his first riddle: 'What is the most fragrant perfume in all creation?'

Princess Chandra replied: 'Sandalwood mixed with Kashmiri saffron.'
Princess Ratna replied: 'Attar of Damascene roses.'
Princess Padma replied: 'Musk from the Himalayan deer.'
Princess Kanti replied: 'The fragrant reputation of an unblemished moral life, which spreads its perfume against the wind and outlives the grave.'

The prince posed his second riddle: 'What is the sharpest weapon in the world?'

Princess Chandra said: 'A tempered steel broadsword.'
Princess Ratna said: 'An iron-tipped arrow shot from a horn-bow.'
Princess Padma said: 'A woman's sidelong glance.'
Princess Kanti replied: 'A harsh, ungrateful word spoken to a loving heart; for arrows pierce only the flesh, but cruel speech wounds the soul forever.'

The prince posed his third riddle: 'What is the greatest wealth in the cosmos?'

Princess Chandra said: 'Caskets of rubies and diamonds.'
Princess Ratna said: 'Vast provinces of fertile land.'
Princess Padma said: 'An invincible army of war-elephants.'
Princess Kanti replied: 'A contented heart that desires nothing that belongs to another, and rests in peace with what duty provides.'

The prince was enraptured by Princess Kanti's wisdom and chose her for his bride.

Here the Vetala asked: 'Tell me, King Vikramaditya: among the four princesses, which one was truly the most beautiful in the eyes of dharma? Speak, or your head will shatter into fragments!'

Vikramaditya replied: 'Princess Kanti was incomparably the most beautiful. The other three princesses were captives of physical sensations—scents, weapons, and gold. Princess Kanti alone possessed the inner vision that sees through the illusions of the senses to the eternal virtues of truth, kindness, and contentment. True beauty resides in the soul, and her wisdom made her the crown of womanhood.'

'Well answered, King!' cried the Vetala, and vanished back to his bough.
moral: Outward beauty fades like morning dew; nobility of character alone endures through the seasons of life.
